source: Lucassen, Dalpiaz, van der Werf, Brinkkemper. Improving Agile Requirements: The Quality User Story Framework and Tool. Requirements Engineering, 2016.

criteria.name: Well-formed
criteria.definition: A user story includes at least a role and a means (the expected functionality).
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when either the stakeholder role or the requested functionality cannot be identified from the core story text.
criteria.lucassen_example: A requirement that only says the user wants to see an error after uploading an article, but omits who the user is, violates Well-formed because the role is missing.

criteria.name: Atomic
criteria.definition: A user story expresses a requirement for exactly one feature.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when the story combines two or more independently implementable, testable, or prioritizable features. Do not flag conjunctions that merely enumerate attributes of one feature.
criteria.lucassen_example: A story that combines clicking a map location with displaying landmarks associated with that location contains two features and should be split.

criteria.name: Minimal
criteria.definition: A user story contains nothing more than role, means, and optional ends/rationale.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when the core story includes comments, mock-up notes, implementation/testing hints, procedural notes, or other information that should be external to the story sentence.
criteria.lucassen_example: A story followed by mock-up notes and step-by-step validation instructions violates Minimal because those notes are extra to role, means, and ends.

criteria.name: Conceptually sound
criteria.definition: The means expresses a feature and the ends expresses a rationale for that feature.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when the means does not state a feature, or when the ends introduces another required feature instead of explaining why the means is valuable.
criteria.lucassen_example: A story whose means is to open an interactive map and whose end is to see landmark locations may make the end function as another feature/dependency rather than a rationale.

criteria.name: Problem-oriented
criteria.definition: A user story specifies the problem or stakeholder need, not the solution to it.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when the story unnecessarily prescribes concrete UI widgets, technical mechanisms, implementation details, algorithms, storage formats, or other solution choices instead of the stakeholder need.
criteria.lucassen_example: A reimbursement story that additionally instructs developers to add a save button at the top right prescribes the solution and violates Problem-oriented.

criteria.name: Unambiguous
criteria.definition: A user story avoids terms or abstractions that lead to multiple materially different interpretations.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when vague, underspecified, overloaded, or unclear terms allow materially different requirements interpretations. Do not flag harmless stylistic variation.
criteria.lucassen_example: A story that says a user can edit 'content' without clarifying what content means is ambiguous when the backlog distinguishes video, photo, and audio content.

criteria.name: Conflict-free
criteria.definition: A user story is not inconsistent with another user story in the same specification.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when two stories impose incompatible permissions, behaviors, constraints, states, or rules. Similarity alone is not a conflict.
criteria.lucassen_example: One story allowing editing of any landmark can conflict with another rule that restricts operations to landmarks created by the current user.

criteria.name: Full sentence
criteria.definition: A user story is a well-formed full sentence.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when the text is a fragment, grammatically incomplete, or malformed enough that it does not read as a complete sentence. Minor typos that do not break sentence completeness should not automatically be defects.
criteria.lucassen_example: A fragment such as 'Server configuration' is not a complete user-story sentence.

criteria.name: Estimatable
criteria.definition: A story does not denote a coarse-grained requirement that is difficult to plan and prioritize.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when scope or behavior is so broad, vague, or underspecified that a reasonable implementation estimate cannot be made. Do not require detailed design before estimation.
criteria.lucassen_example: A request to 'see my route list' can be hard to estimate because it could mean a simple list, route optimization, a map, or several combined capabilities.

criteria.name: Unique
criteria.definition: Every user story is unique; duplicate requirements are avoided.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when another story expresses the same requirement or one is substantially contained in another without a meaningful difference in actor, context, goal, permission, or business rule. Thematic similarity is not enough.
criteria.lucassen_example: An epic and a story that both express the same requirement to view a list of news items are duplicates. Lucassen also notes that the same functionality for different roles can legitimately remain separate.

criteria.name: Uniform
criteria.definition: All user stories in a specification employ the same template.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when a story materially deviates from the dominant user-story template used by its backlog. Compare with the backlog majority rather than enforcing a universal template independent of the dataset.
criteria.lucassen_example: If the backlog predominantly uses 'I want to', a story written as 'I receive an email notification...' may be non-uniform even if its meaning is understandable.

criteria.name: Independent
criteria.definition: The user story is self-contained and has no inherent dependencies on other stories.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when the requested feature inherently depends on another story being implemented first. Do not infer arbitrary technical dependencies; identify a concrete requirement-level dependency and cite the related story.
criteria.lucassen_example: A story for viewing a person's profile depends on a capability for creating a person/profile first, so the dependency should be made explicit.

criteria.name: Complete
criteria.definition: Implementing the set of user stories creates a feature-complete application; crucial steps are not missing.
criteria.decision_rule: Violation when the backlog evidences a necessary complementary capability that is absent, such as update/read/delete behavior whose required creation capability is missing. Attach the violation to the story that exposes the gap and explain the missing complementary requirement.
criteria.lucassen_example: Lucassen illustrates that a story operating on existing content can reveal a completeness gap when no story establishes the creation of that content.
